title: Ghormeh Sabzi
subtitle: Persian herb and lamb stew
excerpt: Ghormeh sabzi is considered Iran's national dish: a deeply aromatic stew of slow-cooked herbs and lamb with a sour, earthy depth that is impossible to rush. The long cooking time is the whole point. Serve with plain basmati rice to soak up the intensely flavoured broth.
sourceNotes: Ghormeh sabzi is considered Iran's national dish, a deeply aromatic stew of slow-cooked herbs and lamb. Dried limes (limu omani) are the key souring agent in the original recipe.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to 3 months.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Ghormeh sabzi deepens in flavour after a day in the refrigerator. Make it the day before for the best results.

content.text: The secret to ghormeh sabzi is patience with the herbs. Frying them in oil before adding any liquid drives off moisture and concentrates their flavour dramatically: the parsley and coriander go from bright green to a deep, almost khaki colour, and that is exactly what you want. The authentic recipe uses dried limes (limu omani): add 3 pierced dried limes with the stock and remove before serving. The juice of 2 lemons approximates that sour depth.

Heat half the olive oil in a large, heavy saucepan over a high heat. Season the lamb with salt and the turmeric. Brown the lamb in batches, making sure not to crowd the pan: each piece needs good colour on at least two sides. Set aside.

Reduce the heat to medium. Add the remaining olive oil to the pan and tip in the chopped parsley, coriander, and spinach. Fry, stirring frequently, for 15 to 20 minutes until the herbs are very dark and fragrant. This step is not optional: it is what gives ghormeh sabzi its characteristic depth.

Return the browned lamb to the pan and stir to combine with the herbs. Pour in enough cold water to cover by about 3 cm (roughly 600 to 700 ml). Bring to the boil, then skim off any foam that rises to the surface.
Reduce the heat to a very low simmer, cover the pan, and cook for 1 hour 30 minutes, checking occasionally that the liquid has not reduced too far. Add a splash more water if the stew looks dry.
Add the drained kidney beans and lemon juice. Stir gently, replace the lid, and continue to cook for a further 30 minutes until the lamb is completely tender and falling apart.

Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and more lemon juice if needed. The stew should taste deeply savoury and pleasingly sour. The sauce should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon: if it is still loose, simmer uncovered for a further 10 minutes.
Serve with plain steamed basmati rice. Ghormeh sabzi improves significantly if left overnight and reheated gently the next day.

items.symptom: The stew tastes flat and lacks depth
items.cause: The herbs were not fried long enough. Under-fried herbs produce a thin, grassy flavour rather than the concentrated, almost meaty intensity the dish needs.
items.fix: Continue frying the herb mixture well beyond the point where it looks done. Dark and slightly sticky is correct; green and bright is not.

items.symptom: The lamb is still tough after the cooking time
items.cause: Lamb shoulder needs sustained gentle heat to break down its connective tissue. High heat toughens the meat rather than softening it.
items.fix: Keep the lid on and continue to cook at a very low simmer for another 30 minutes. Check the liquid level and add water as needed.

items.cause: The ratio of liquid to solids was too high, or the lid was kept on throughout, preventing any reduction.
items.fix: Remove the lid and simmer over a medium heat for 10 to 15 minutes until the sauce reduces to a thick, coating consistency.
